problem: VLM navigation agents fail through trajectory-level breakdowns (oscillation, stagnation, detours), but existing uncertainty proxies (action entropy, token confidence, conformal residuals) capture only instantaneous decision ambiguity and cannot anticipate these failures. There is also no protocol for evaluating episode-level uncertainty ranking independently of task success.
motivation: Reliable deployment needs a runtime signal indicating whether an ongoing trajectory deviates from goal-directed execution. Distance-to-goal is a readily available, model-agnostic geometric signal that evolves smoothly in successful episodes and shows detectable inconsistency in failing ones.
key_idea: Model distance-to-goal with a constant-velocity Kalman filter and fuse its normalized innovation and posterior covariance statistics with trajectory features (progress, monotonicity, path efficiency, action reversals) into a fixed-weight episode uncertainty score, evaluated by a selective risk-coverage protocol (SRCN).
insight: Geometric progress dynamics rank failures far better than instantaneous action dispersion, especially on long-horizon episodes where entropy and conformal signals approach random ordering (AURC_SR long_horizon GPT-4o: GroundControl 0.55 vs Entropy 0.90, Random 0.83). The gain comes with fixed hand-set weights and no learning. However, no ablation of the individual components is provided, so the contribution of the Kalman terms versus the simple trajectory features is not isolated.
method: Constant-velocity KF: state [d_t, d_dot_t], F=[[1,1],[0,1]], H=[1 0]; init Σ0=diag(0.01,1.0); yields innovation ν_t and covariance S_t; NIS ν²/S is a chi-square(1) consistency test.
Per-step score H_t = 1.0·logdet(Σ_t|t+εI) + 0.5·Bernoulli entropy of executed-action confidence + 0.8·ν²/S; episode KF score = sigmoid(max_t H_t).
Trajectory features in [0,1]: f_prog (insufficient net distance reduction), f_mono (non-decreasing steps fraction), f_eff (path inefficiency), f_osc (action-reversal frequency).
Fixed linear fusion U_i with weights (skf, prog, mono, eff, osc) = (0.30, 0.25, 0.20, 0.15, 0.10); no learned weights.
SRCN protocol: sort episodes by U_i, compute selective risk (1-Succ or 1-SPL) vs coverage, AURC via trapezoid rule, E-AURC = AURC minus oracle AURC, optional ECE.
Active recovery (not evaluated): switching controller between task/recover/halt policies at thresholds (0.35, 0.65) on running max score.

setting.backbone: GPT-4o, GPT-5-mini, Gemini-1.5-Flash (frozen VLM navigation policies); GroundControl is a post-hoc hand-designed estimator (Kalman filter + fixed features)
setting.training_data: none (training-free, fixed weights, evaluated post hoc on fixed trajectories)
setting.observation: egocentric RGB observation with language instruction; distance-to-goal signal and executed-action confidence used by the estimator
setting.action_space: 8 discrete actions (forward, backward, left, right, rotate-left/right, look-up/down), 0.25 m step
setting.privileged: Ground-truth distance-to-goal at every step used by the uncertainty estimator; oracle ordering used only for E-AURC

numbers_note: The benchmark is not a canonical one, so 'other:EB-Navigation' is used and the split is labelled 'test' as a placeholder. The paper reports uncertainty-ranking metrics, not new navigation SR. Underlying agent performance is in Table 1 (e.g. GPT-4o success 58.3/58.3/56.7/53.3/16.7%). The abstract's weighted-average E-AURC_SR=0.0024 is not in the tables, which print 0.00.
results: GroundControl achieves near-oracle failure ranking on EB-Navigation: E-AURC_SR of 0.00 on most splits and 0.01 on long_horizon, versus 0.19 (Entropy), 0.40 (Conformal), 0.18 (Self-Consist.) and 0.28 (Random) for GPT-4o on average. Under SPL-based risk it has the best averages for GPT-4o and Gemini. For GPT-5-mini, Entropy ties or slightly beats it on some splits (e.g. base AURC_SPL 0.10 vs 0.12).
limitations: Small evaluation: 60 episodes per split, one simulator (EB-Navigation), no ablations of KF vs. features and no sensitivity study of the hand-set weights.
Requires ground-truth distance-to-goal at every step, which is unavailable in real deployment. It is also evaluated post hoc over whole episodes, and the active-recovery controller is not tested.
The baselines are weak, simple episode-level heuristics rather than learned failure predictors. Features such as path efficiency may partly exploit correlation with episode length and failure.
